title: Song of songs, dance of dances
hookLine: salutation to the song within songs, the sound within sounds, the dance within dances (Jaap)

lines: A BACKYARD, A SONG EVERYONE KNOWS.
cards: A backyard, late on a Saturday. Somebody puts on an old song, the kind everybody's aunt knows. One person starts nodding.

Someone taps a spoon on the table. Then a grandfather who hasn't danced since the last wedding lifts one hand and turns his wrist, just once, and the whole yard laughs and joins in. Nobody decided to dance.
The song did it. Something in music moves people before they choose to move, and Jaap Sahib salutes whatever that is.

teach.b: Near the sun of suns, Jaap keeps doubling words, and now it reaches sound. Salutation to the song within songs. To naad naade, the sound within sounds.
To the dance within dances. Not a better song, but the song inside every song, the thing that makes music move us at all.
Naad means sound, and in Gurbani it often means the deep sound of the Divine, the music under everything, heard by whoever listens closely. Music isn't decoration in Sikh life; it's the main road.

teach.h: THE GRANTH IS ARRANGED BY RAAG.
teach.b: The Guru Granth Sahib is arranged by raag, by musical mode, so its hymns are grouped by the way they're meant to be sung.
Sikh tradition remembers that Guru Nanak traveled with a musician, Bhai Mardana, who played the rabab while the Guru sang. Kirtan, singing the Guru's words, is at the heart of the gurdwara.
Dance is different: worship in the gurdwara is sung, not danced. But Jaap isn't describing a ritual here.

teach.h: THE MOVEMENT IN ALL MOVING THINGS.
teach.b: It bows to the movement in all moving things: the sway of a field of wheat, the turning of the seasons, that grandfather's wrist.

And the week ends here. Seven days in Jaap: akaal, the Timeless; kripaal, the Merciful; aroop, formless and beyond compare; ajooni, unborn; the armed One, the protector; the sun of suns. And today, the song in every song.

how: Music is central to Sikh worship: the Guru Granth Sahib is arranged by raag, and kirtan, singing its hymns with harmonium and tabla, fills the gurdwara; worship itself is sung rather than danced.

games.q: Guru Nanak sets out on long journeys to share his hymns. who travels with him?
o: a scribe to write it all down.
a musician, Bhai Mardana, with his rabab.
games.why: Bhai Mardana played the rabab while the Guru sang: in Sikh life, music is the main road, not decoration.

practice: Play or hum one song you love, a shabad, a hymn, something from your childhood, and let one part of you move with it: a foot, a hand, a slow sway. Notice the moment the music starts moving you, rather than you moving to it.
When it ends, sit still with the quiet it leaves.

wordCard.voice: Naad. Sound, the deep sound of the Divine — in Jaap's doubled salutations, a bow to the song within every song, the dance within dance.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: naad, sound; in Gurbani often the deep sound of the Divine. Jaap doubles it: naad naade.

carryVoice: Your line: the dance of dances. Every song has a song inside it. A week, done: see you tomorrow.
